name: PT Widodo Makmur Unggas Tbk

frontmatter.title: Widodo Makmur Unggas: the recapitalisation is scheduled, and the equity is still worth nothing
frontmatter.summary: WMUU restructured its debt, not its economics. The rights issue is approved and scheduled, and we model it at its proforma maximum. Even so, the cash flows do not produce an enterprise value that clears the post-rights net debt, and the price pays for an asset sale well above what the operating business earns. SELL.
thesis: The data pack understates depreciation tenfold and reports a higher operating profit than the filing; on the audited numbers WMUU earned an EBITDA margin of under three per cent in FY2025 against an interest bill that consumed more than all of it.

The PMHMETD I rights issue was approved in April 2026, with the OJK declaration effective in June and the memorandum scheduling trading for July: 6.0 bn new shares at Rp100, IDR600.5bn of new net assets, the parent undertaking to pay for its entitlement by converting its shareholder loan. We model that proforma maximum, which is the most favourable case for the equity; the proceeds sit in the valuation bridge and are not assumed to have been received [S13].
Even with the full proceeds credited, enterprise value on our DCF is below the net debt it must clear, and the same is true on the peer multiple applied to restated FY2025 EBITDA.

On our FY2026E net debt the price is 74.0x our FY2026E EBITDA, and it stays many times the 4.9x the peer set pays even after the maximum rights proceeds are credited, for a business whose EBIT has been negative in every year since FY2023. The same calculation on the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet net debt, which is lower than our FY2026E forecast, is a lower multiple for that reason alone.

Governance is weak: a qualified audit opinion, a court-supervised settlement, an OJK fine for an affiliate-transaction procedure breach, uninsured fixed assets and a parent that is creditor, controlling shareholder and subscriber at once.

blocks.text: **SELL. Target Rp0, a return of -100.0% from Rp49.** The engine renders the zero target against the current print; because the exchange's minimum price is Rp1 [S8], the reachable return is about minus ninety-eight per cent, and that floor return, not the arithmetic minus-one-hundred, is what a holder can act on. This is an initiation revised after review, and the correction runs against our previous draft rather than for it. We had excluded the rights issue on the grounds that the meeting called to approve it failed quorum. The primary documents show otherwise: the PMHMETD I was approved at a general meeting held in April 2026, the OJK declaration became effective in June, and the information memorandum schedules the rights to trade in early July, with the new shares to be distributed the same month [S13][F24][F27]. We model the issue at its proforma maximum, in every scenario. We value the equity at nothing, because the operating business valued on its own cash flows at a cost of capital of 12.0% does not produce an enterprise value large enough to clear the net debt it sits behind [S0][S10].

The variant view is about the operating line, and it cuts both ways. The audited accounts show a loss from operations of IDR-45.0bn and a depreciation charge of 65.4 IDR bn, of which IDR5.9bn was charged to operating expenses and the balance to cost of goods sold [S10]. The data pack carries only that operating-expense slice, a tenth of the real charge, and reports a higher operating profit than the filing. Restating both turns the pack's EBITDA loss into a positive IDR20.4bn, an EBITDA margin of 2.8%, and the same definition of EBIT runs through the forecast [S0][S10]. That is the honest starting point, and it is still not enough: interest expense was IDR38.6bn [S0].

Three things move the value, and only one of them is operational. The first is the debt: with net debt of IDR1,252.5bn at the 2025 year-end, lower but still large at the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date after the first-half asset-for-debt exchange, and against which the maximum IDR600.5bn of rights proceeds is credited as a bridge item, the equity only becomes valuable once enterprise value clears that line. Even after that credit the remaining net debt is still about three-fifths of the IDR634.1bn market capitalisation the pack prints on the pre-issue count, and the pack's own count does not include the rights shares [S0][S13]. The second is the gross margin. On our forecast revenue rises to IDR1,000.3bn in FY2026 and IDR1,424.1bn in FY2030, yet modelled EBIT is IDR-39.5bn in FY2026 and IDR-47.8bn in FY2030, because the margin the model actually earns after the feed links - 0.4% in FY2026 and 1.0% in FY2030 - is below operating costs of 4.3% of sales [S0][S10]. The third is the balance-sheet event, and it has been approved but not evidenced: the parent undertook to take its 40.9% entitlement by converting its receivable, which is why we credit the proceeds in the bridge; it does not change the operating economics [S13].

We are deliberately not taking the cautious path. We assume the rights issue completes in full at its documented maximum, which is the most favourable assumption available for the equity [S13]; we assume the demand recovery continues at the run-rate the first half established [S0]; and we assume part of the feed-cost increase is passed through at 65.0% of the corn move, a judgement we state as a judgement rather than as a disclosed rate [S9][S10]. On those assumptions the equity is worth nothing. What the price pays for is something the model cannot see: a buyer for the assets at close to book, which no filing supports.

WMUU is a vertically integrated Indonesian poultry processor. It operates a feedmill, a broiler breeding and hatchery operation, commercial broiler farms and a slaughter and carcass business, and it sells eggs [S9]. The company began commercial production in 2017 and listed in 2020; it is controlled by PT Widodo Makmur Perkasa, which is itself listed and separately restructuring its own debt [S9][S6]. Production is marketed inside Indonesia, with no export base [S10].

The revenue mix matters more than the description, because it explains why the margins are so thin. In FY2025 the carcass segment sold 643 IDR bn of a consolidated IDR740.9bn, with eggs, day-old chicks, feed and commercial broilers making up the rest [S10]. Carcass is a commodity product: the company buys live birds in the open market, slaughters them and sells chicken meat at a price it does not set. The upstream businesses are small in revenue terms but carry most of the margin, with the day-old-chick and feed segments out-earning carcass at the gross-profit level in FY2025 while the commercial broiler operation lost money [S9][S10].

The operating footprint has shrunk hard. Feedmill output fell to 1,464 t in FY2025, a collapse of the feed trading business that had been the group's revenue engine before FY2023 [S9]. Against that, hatchery output rose to 4.4 m birds and egg production to 37.3 m eggs [S9]. The shape of the company has changed: it is now a slaughter and egg business with a shrunken feed operation, not the feed-led integrator it was at listing.

Strategy, as the company describes it, is utilisation and diversification rather than expansion. The FY2025 annual report sets out resizing the broiler population, diversifying into commercial layer production, completing or divesting the stalled construction projects, and restructuring the debt [S10]. The company states that it made no capital investment in FY2025 [S9]. Management is explicit that feed prices rising into early 2025 raised its cost of production, and that the remedy is efficiency, marketing restraint and cash preservation rather than volume growth at any price [S10].

The competitive position is that of a sub-scale challenger. The Indonesian poultry industry is dominated by integrated producers with national distribution and branded consumer products; WMUU sells commodity carcass and eggs into wholesale markets where the regional price is set by supply [S9][S10]. It has no brand pricing power, no export business and, at present, no ability to invest. Its one real asset advantage is a large, modern, under-utilised fixed-asset base of 2,124 IDR bn net book value, which is a source of operating leverage if volumes return and a source of losses if they do not [S10].

Group structure is simple and that is part of the problem. PT Widodo Makmur Perkasa controls the listed subsidiary with 40.9% of the shares, is the largest creditor through a shareholder loan of 406 IDR bn, and has undertaken to subscribe to the rights issue by converting that claim into equity at Rp100 a share against a market price of Rp49 [S10][S13]. Minorities are immaterial on the balance sheet [S0]. The 2,124 IDR bn asset base runs on a fraction of the volume it was built for, which is itself evidence of how little of it is working [S0][S10].

The Indonesian poultry chain runs from imported feed grains through feedmills to breeding, hatchery,
broiler growing and finally slaughter and cold chain. Live-bird and carcass prices are set daily in
regional markets and are volatile; feed is the dominant cost, so the industry's margin is effectively
the spread between feed grain and chicken, captured or lost depending on how much of the chain a
producer owns and how well it times bird placement. Government food programmes and price interventions
move demand and the retail price, but not the underlying spread. Firms that own the whole chain can
smooth the spread; firms that buy birds in the open market, as this one largely does for its slaughter
business, cannot.

The industry's problem in the period covered by these accounts was oversupply. The company's own disclosure describes oversupply in early 2024 driving day-old-chick and live-bird prices down, a partial recovery in the second quarter and then oversupply again through the third and fourth quarters, with chick prices falling back [S10]. That is the mechanism behind the collapse in WMUU's revenue and margins: it is a price-taker in a market that spent two years digesting excess bird numbers.

The cost side has moved the other way. The house agricultural deck carries corn at US$215/t for FY2027 against a spot of US$175/t, and soymeal at US$411/t against a spot of US$364/t. The deck therefore has feed grains above spot and rising from here, not falling, and the model carries that series through every forecast year rather than reverting to spot after the reviewed years: where the reviewed series ends it is extended at the deck's own long-run rate. That is the mechanism behind the gap between the base-input gross margin of 5.5% in FY2030 and the 1.0% the model actually earns. For a processor whose gross margin is a few percentage points, feed cost is the single most important external variable, and it is why our margin path improves only slowly even as revenue recovers [S0][S10].

Demand, by contrast, has a policy tailwind. The company points to national protein demand and to government food assistance programmes as the reason the poultry sector should recover, and to cage-free egg development as an adjacent opportunity [S9]. The parent's own disclosure for the first quarter of 2026 attributes its swing back to profit to poultry, which it says accounted for the large majority of group revenue, and names the free nutritious meals programme as a demand driver [S6]. That is consistent with the recovery in WMUU's quarterly revenue through FY2026 [S0]. It is a real tailwind and we take it seriously; it is also a demand tailwind every producer in the country faces, so it supports volume rather than pricing.

Regulation and supervision matter more here than in a normal consumer name. The company went through a court-supervised debt payment suspension, a PKPU, from July 2024 in the Central Jakarta commercial court, and obtained approval of a settlement proposal [S9]. The settlement imposes creditor oversight: a six-monthly joint review of a divestment programme, with the company committed to completing or divesting five assets under construction by the fourth quarter of 2027, funded through a rights issue, a bond issue or share divestment [S10]. In November 2026 the financial services authority fined the company 925 IDR m for failing to follow the material and affiliate transaction procedure on a loan it received [S2][S4][S7]. Separately, the stock is a penny-priced name on the exchange's gocap list, for which the minimum traded price was cut to one rupiah from late September 2026 [S8]. That is a market-structure fact, not a finding of wrongdoing, but it caps the downside a holder can actually realise and it tells you who is left in the register: a share that could not be sold at the old floor now can be sold at the new one, which is relief for sellers and no support for the price.

On the five forces the picture is weak across the board. Supplier power is high: feed grains are imported and priced globally, and the company is a price-taker. Buyer power is high: carcass and egg buyers are wholesale traders who can switch supplier by the truckload. Rivalry is intense and the industry has been in oversupply. The threat of substitutes is low in the short run because chicken is the cheapest animal protein in Indonesia, which is the one genuinely favourable force [S0]. Barriers to entry are moderate in growing and slaughter but high for the integrated asset base WMUU already owns, which is precisely why those assets are worth more to a better-capitalised operator than to this balance sheet.

Market share is small and, on the company's own numbers, shrinking in feed and stable in slaughter [S9][S10]. The moat assessment is therefore straightforward: no pricing power, no switching costs, no brand, no distribution advantage, and a cost position that depends on bird and grain prices it does not control. What it has is capacity. Capacity is a call option on the cycle, and it is financed with debt.

The industry also consolidates around scale in a way that penalises this company specifically. A processor with a national footprint can balance birds across regions when one market is oversupplied; WMUU's footprint is concentrated and its feed business, the natural hedge against grain prices, has shrunk to almost nothing [S9]. That is why the same industry cycle that a larger integrator rides out took this company into a court-supervised restructuring.

**The revenue history is a collapse and a recovery, not a growth story.** Revenue fell from IDR2,457.6bn in FY2022 to IDR336.7bn in FY2023 and IDR378.1bn in FY2024, then recovered 95.9% to IDR740.9bn in FY2025 [S0][S9]. The collapse was the feed trading business disappearing, with feedmill output now a small fraction of its former level [S9]; the recovery is carcass and egg volume coming back as the market absorbed the oversupply [S0][S10].

**Margins.** The reported gross margin was -1.7% in FY2025, an improvement from a deep loss in FY2024 [S0]. At the segment level, before unallocated costs, the operating segments earned a positive gross profit in FY2025 - 643 IDR bn of carcass revenue inside a consolidated total that still lost money at the gross line - so the consolidated loss is driven by costs the company cannot allocate to a product line, largely the carrying cost of capacity it is not using [S10]. Our base case sets the base-input margin at 4.0% in FY2026 rising to 5.5% in FY2030, which is the segment margin before the feed links; the margin the model actually earns after the corn and soymeal links is 0.4% in FY2026 and 1.0% in FY2030. The uplift from the FY2025 consolidated margin is sourced to the segment disclosure [S10]; the shortfall against the input is the feed-cost link [S0].

**One definition of operating profit, for history and forecast.** EBIT in this model is the filing's own operating line, not the vendor's: the FY2025 consolidated LK reports a loss from operations of IDR-45.0bn, struck after cost of goods sold IDR753.8bn, operating expenses, other expenses (the allowance for doubtful accounts and the residual value of culled birds) and other income (the sale of culled birds) [S10]. Those other lines sit above the operating result, not below it, so the model's operating-cost line is the whole block above the line - IDR32.2bn in FY2025 - and gross profit less that line equals the LK's operating result in FY2024 and FY2025, the two years restated from the filing, and in every forecast year. The same definition is applied to FY2024, where the LK's operating loss was IDR-94.9bn [S10]. FY2022 and FY2023 are the exception: we hold no archived LK for either year, so those two years remain the data pack's operating profit, which puts the doubtful-account and culled-bird lines in a different place and is not comparable line for line with the restated years [S0][S10]. We say so wherever those years are used, and we do not restate them by inference.

**Depreciation, restated.** The audited accounts show the charge is 65.4 IDR bn for FY2025 and 57.0 IDR bn for FY2024, split between cost of goods sold and operating expenses [S10]. The IDR5.9bn charged to operating expenses is what the data pack carries; the much larger portion charged to cost of goods sold is missing [S0][S10]. The restatement is ours, not the company's, and it is sourced to the fixed-asset note of the FY2025 accounts. The engine rebuilds history from it, so EBITDA is IDR20.4bn in FY2025 and IDR-38.0bn in FY2024, both the LK's operating result plus the full depreciation charge, and the model reproduces the filing within rounding rather than the vendor's higher operating profit [S0][S10]. Restating does not flatter cash generation; it clarifies that the business does generate a little EBITDA, and that the assets are being consumed at a rate the pack did not show. On the restated numbers the fixed-asset base of 2,124 IDR bn is about thirty years of depreciation, which for poultry housing, plant and equipment is too long a life and implies further impairment risk [S10].

**Costs and operating leverage.** The operating-cost block above the operating line was IDR32.2bn in FY2025, 4.3% of sales, and the forecast holds that ratio flat. We do not strip the other income and expense lines out of it, because the filing carries them above the operating result and they recurred in FY2024 as well: the allowance for doubtful accounts and the culled-bird charge are operating costs of this business, not a one-off [S10]. History and forecast therefore use the same block, and gross profit less this line is the LK's operating result in the two restated years and in every forecast year; FY2022 and FY2023 are the pack's un-restated operating profit, as set out above. This is the crux of the investment case: with a gross margin of 0.4% after feed costs and operating costs at 4.3% of sales, EBIT is structurally negative. Modelled EBIT is IDR-39.5bn in FY2026, still IDR-47.8bn in FY2030 and IDR-95.9bn by FY2035 as feed costs squeeze the margin [S0]. The company does not earn its cost of capital on the assets it owns, and has not done so since FY2022, when revenue was three times today's and EBIT was IDR80.8bn on the data pack's un-restated operating profit [S0].

**The June quarter is the bear point.** The second quarter of 2026 is the period to read. Revenue was flat on the first quarter, operating expenses jumped to several times the March level - the largest operating-cost quarter in the series - and EBIT fell to a loss several times the first quarter's. The reported net profit for the quarter was positive only because of non-operating items, with a tax benefit against a pre-tax loss [S0]. Trailing-twelve-month EBIT to June is therefore a larger loss than the whole of FY2025, and trailing EBITDA to June is negative, against the IDR25.9bn our FY2026 forecast requires. The recovery visible in the pack is a recovery in revenue, not in operating profit. The base case requires the second half of FY2026 to earn an EBITDA margin above the first half's; the June quarter is the evidence against that, which is why the benefit of the doubt sits in the bull case rather than the base.

**The September quarter in the pack is unusable, and we do not model it.** The refreshed data pack's September 2026 quarter is internally inconsistent: it books a credit inside operating expenses larger than the quarter's entire revenue, so EBIT and EBITDA come out above the quarter revenue while profit before tax is negative [S0]. The same credit inflates the pack's trailing-twelve-month EBITDA to many times the audited FY2025 figure, so the pack's LTM is not a usable operating series [S0]. The company has not published a Q3-2026 report on its investor-relations site - the latest filing there is the audited FY2025 accounts - so there is no filing to correct the vendor from [S3][S10]. We therefore keep the engine on an annual basis: its history is the audited FY2025A lines restated from the LK, the forecast starts from those lines, and the engine replaces the pack's LTM revenue, EBITDA and net profit with the restated FY2025A values before valuing the company [S0][S10]. The only pack figure we use from the September quarter is the balance sheet, which is internally consistent and is the latest available debt and equity position; the valuation therefore opens on 30 September 2026. We flag the P&L quarter as a vendor defect rather than model around it.

**Cash flow and capex.** Operating cash flow was 4.4 IDR bn in FY2025 under the direct method, with capital expenditure of 5.9 IDR bn [S10]. The company states it made no capital investment in FY2025 [S9], and the trailing twelve months to June 2026 show a similar run-rate of roughly one per cent of revenue [S0]. That is not sustainable in the long run, but it is what the company does, and it is why the previous note's capex line - several times revenue and ten times the last actual - was wrong. The capex that the settlement actually requires is the completion cost of the five construction projects, carried at 35.8 IDR bn at about half complete on average with a Q4-2027 deadline: about thirty-three billion rupiah left to spend, or roughly one and a half per cent of FY2026 revenue a year across FY2026 and FY2027 [S10]. Our forecast sets capex at 2.5% of revenue in FY2026 and FY2027 on that basis, rising to 4.0% by FY2030 and the restated depreciation ratio in the long run, which is the restated depreciation charge - a going concern must eventually replace what it consumes. On that path free cash flow is IDR8.1bn in FY2026, positive because the capex line is no longer ten times the last actual and because depreciation, a non-cash charge, now sits properly inside EBITDA [S0].

**Balance sheet and debt.** The valuation's opening balance sheet is the 30 September 2026 pack, the latest available: it shows net debt below the IDR1,252.5bn of the prior year-end, alongside a fall in net fixed assets of similar magnitude and little change in equity, which is the arithmetic of assets being transferred or settled rather than of cash repaying debt [S0]. The company has not published its Q2- or Q3-2026 accounts on its investor-relations site, so the mechanism cannot be sourced from a filing; we say so rather than invent one, and we use the September net debt where it belongs, as the DCF's opening net debt [S3][S0]. The forecast itself rolls the audited 31 December 2025 balance sheet: net debt goes from IDR1,252.5bn to IDR1,283.3bn in FY2026. The bridge is IDR18.6bn of net new borrowing - the deferred interest, the operating loss and maintenance capex funded through creditor forbearance and the shareholder loan - plus the fall in the cash line from IDR1.7bn to IDR-10.5bn - the audited net debt plus the new borrowing plus the cash decline equals the forecast net debt of IDR1,283.3bn. The rights proceeds are not part of it: they sit in the valuation bridge and are never added to forecast cash [S0][S10]. The template has no equity-issuance or disposal line: booking the first-half asset-for-debt exchange as negative capex would count a one-off disposal as free cash flow in the DCF, so it is captured once, at the valuation date, and not again in the forecast [S0]. We do not plug cash to a floor. The borrowing input records the new debt the settlement and the parent's support can carry, not an unbounded overdraft, and the residual funding gap shows up as a negative cash balance - IDR-10.5bn in FY2026 and IDR-206.2bn by FY2035 - which is disclosed here rather than smoothed away [S0][S10]. Both paths are presentation, not a value assumption: the DCF is unlevered free cash flow, so the debt and cash path affects only interest and the balance sheet. The consequence is stated plainly: equity rolls to IDR-275.4bn by FY2035, so the forecast is insolvent on paper before the terminal year. The ROE line then becomes meaningless - it reads 77.9% on a negative equity base - and we do not use a book-based valuation. The interest charge also assumes the settlement's concessional 3.1% cost of debt for the whole forecast with no step-up; a market cost of debt would lower equity further, so that assumption flatters the equity, not the reverse [S10]. Against equity of IDR774.4bn the company reports a debt-to-equity ratio of 200.0% on its own measure [S9][S10]. The debt is not a bank-only problem: 406 IDR bn is a shareholder loan from the parent, unchanged year on year, and it is more than half of book equity [S10]. The rest is restructured bank debt, a non-bank financial institution facility, lease obligations, accrued interest and trade payables [S10]. Cash interest paid in FY2025 was a small fraction of the interest expense because the settlement defers it [S10]; that is liquidity relief, not solvency relief, and the interest still accrues against equity. Net debt is 61.4 times restated EBITDA, and because the forecast funds its own deficit with debt while EBITDA does not grow, it is 87.9 times by FY2030 [S0].

**The recapitalisation, scheduled but not evidenced.** The PMHMETD I was approved at the general meeting of April 2026, and the OJK declaration became effective in June [S13][F24]. It offers 6.0 bn new shares, about a third of the post-issue capital, on the ratio and record date set out in the prospectus, at an exercise price of Rp100, for maximum proceeds of IDR600.5bn [S13]. The information memorandum of 16 April 2026 schedules HMETD trading for early July 2026, with distribution of the resulting shares the same month [S13][F27]. No allotment result or paid-up-capital filing is archived, so execution is scheduled and undertaken rather than evidenced, and the post-issue count of 18,946 m shares is the proforma structure [S13]. The controlling shareholder undertook in writing in April 2026 to take its entire 40.9% entitlement and to pay by converting its receivable [S13], so the parent is a subscriber to its entitlement rather than the sole subscriber: the balance is offered to the other holders. The proceeds are earmarked for working capital, with the converted portion extinguishing debt [S13]. Two things follow. First, the share count is nearly half again as large as the pack shows (the new shares are about a third of the post-issue count), so the market capitalisation the pack reports is computed on the old count. Second, the exercise price is twice the market price, so a minority holder has no reason to exercise; we model the issue in full anyway, which is the most favourable case for the equity and the one that cannot be criticised as a cautious assumption [S13].

**Earnings-quality flags.** On the house screen, the accruals picture is not the problem: the company is loss-making and operating cash flow tracks the loss, so there is no Sloan-type flag. The real flags are structural. First, the depreciation understatement in the data source, which flatters EBITDA by an order of magnitude in the pack; we have restated it [S10]. Second, the fixed assets were uninsured at the balance-sheet date [S10], so a fire or disease event would be an unhedged loss against a 2,124 IDR bn asset base. Third, related-party gravity: a shareholder loan of 406 IDR bn plus related party receivables and payables, a regulator sanction for skipping the affiliate transaction procedure on a loan [S2][S10], and a rights issue in which the controlling shareholder has undertaken to convert its own claim into equity at twice the market price [S13]. Fourth, a qualified audit opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S9]. Fifth, the June quarter: an operating-cost spike with a positive net profit underneath it is the pattern to watch, not to extrapolate [S0]. None of these is a fabrication finding; together they describe a control environment that warrants a discount, not the benefit of the doubt.

**Forecast summary.** Revenue IDR1,000.3bn in FY2026 rising to IDR1,424.1bn in FY2030, EBITDA IDR25.9bn to IDR17.5bn, EBIT negative in every forecast year, no dividend, and net debt rising from IDR1,252.5bn to IDR1,542.2bn because the forecast funds its own cash shortfall with debt and the residual with a negative cash balance (IDR-81.6bn by FY2030, IDR-206.2bn by FY2035), as disclosed above [S0][S10]. The engine's calibration check prices FY2026 at FY2025 conditions and puts FY2026 EBITDA margin within a fifth of a percentage point of the FY2025 actual of 2.8%, so the forecast reproduces the last actual year's cost economics rather than a hoped-for improvement: history and forecast carry the same operating-cost block. What is left is the gross margin, -1.7% in FY2025 against 0.4% modelled for FY2026 after the feed links. That is the recovery assumption, stated openly.

We value WMUU on discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check. The compounder card's default set also includes a P/E weight; we have removed it and moved its weight to the other two methods, because the company has posted losses in each of the last four fiscal years and there is no positive forward EPS to put a multiple on [S0]. A price-to-book cross-check is shown for context but not weighted: book equity of IDR774.4bn is carried at a fixed-asset value of 2,124 IDR bn that has never been tested by a sale, and construction-in-progress carrying values make book a poor guide to realisable value [S10].

The cost of capital is 12.0%. The cost of equity of 19.2% is built from a risk-free rate of 7.4% less the engine's default credit spread of 1.6%, plus a levered beta of 1.99 applied to the sum of a mature equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%. That is the engine's convention and the decomposition reproduces the reported cost of equity exactly: the sovereign default spread is netted out of the IDR risk-free rate, and the country premium is applied through the beta rather than added as a separate term. The beta is the industry asset beta of 0.90 relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.56, which is where a distressed capital structure belongs. The weights follow the actual capital structure, with debt at 60.9% of the funding against 39.1% of equity [S0][S10]. The pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% is the risk-free rate plus the debt spread, which is the right market rate for a distressed borrower; the rate actually accruing under the settlement is lower because the settlement froze it, and that gap is a subsidy from creditors to equity, not a lower cost of capital [S10]. The 12.0% result sits mid-band for IDR names rather than at the top of it; the leverage and the earnings record justify the upper half of the band, and the relevered beta of 1.99 is what puts it there.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR-555.7bn before the rights proceeds: on our forecast the operating business is worth less than nothing. The IDR600.5bn of rights proceeds sit in the bridge, against net debt at the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date; the bridge reduces the shortfall but does not eliminate it, and the DCF's equity value is negative both before and after the bridge [S0][S13]. We do not hide the construction. Free cash flow is positive in the explicit period only in its first year (FY2026), because capex sits below the depreciation charge early on; by the terminal year capex converges on depreciation, as a going concern requires, and the FY2035 free cash flow of IDR-77.4bn is negative. Growing that negative flow at the 4.0% terminal growth rate produces a terminal value that is 64.6% of the enterprise value and makes the perpetuity more negative, not less. That terminal is not a steady state: a growing perpetuity of negative free cash flow is the arithmetic of a business that cannot continue as a going concern, where the economic terminal is closure and the formula attaches a negative value to an outcome whose true floor is the salvage value of the assets. We therefore read it as a going-concern failure marker, not as a sale value. The closure case is the zero-terminal sensitivity, and it is disclosed: remove the terminal and the enterprise value is the present value of the explicit forecast alone, which is higher than the reported DCF enterprise value because the perpetuity it removes is negative, and is still far below the post-proceeds net debt, so the equity remains worthless without the floor. The zero target does not depend on the terminal. The engine has no exit-multiple terminal; the compounder card's survival test can still be run against it. Applying the 4.9x peer entry multiple to terminal-year EBITDA of IDR-15.9bn gives an exit enterprise value of only a fraction of the IDR1,252.5bn net debt at the last audited date, and terminal-year EBIT of IDR-95.9bn is negative, so no positive exit EV/EBIT exists to compare with the entry multiple. The multiple-survival test fails on every leg.

The asset-value test is the one that matters for a levered, asset-heavy name, and it is the cross-check the red team asked for. The audited fixed-asset base is 2,124 IDR bn against total debt of IDR1,254.2bn at the same date, so recovering the debt at carrying value takes about three-fifths of the fixed-asset base before any value is left for land, licences or the equity; and the base has fallen since the 2025 year-end as the first-half asset-for-debt exchange removed assets [S0][S10]. That is the debt-recovery test, and it is why the equity is worth nothing when the operating business cannot service the debt: the assets cover the creditors, not the shareholders. Per share the DCF is negative before the limited-liability floor, and the floor is what the target is: an equity whose enterprise value does not cover its net debt is worth nothing, and the exchange's minimum price of Rp1 is a trading rule, not a valuation [S8].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check says the same thing from the other side. The engine applies 4.9x - the median of the five poultry and protein peers that carry the metric, CPIN, CPRO, JPFA, MAIN and SIPD - to restated FY2025 EBITDA of IDR20.4bn, giving an enterprise value higher than the DCF and still a fraction of the net debt the equity sits behind [S0]. Applied to FY2026E EBITDA of IDR25.9bn instead, the same multiple leaves the equity negative. The metric matters: it is the restated actual, not our forecast, so the cross-check does not depend on the recovery assumption at all.

The sensitivity grid is the honest answer to what would have to change, and it now varies the drivers that matter rather than only the discount rate. Across a two-percentage-point band of WACC and terminal growth the per-share value does not leave zero in the base or bear case, because enterprise value never approaches net debt [S0]. What would move it is not a discount rate: it is either an operating margin this company has never earned, or an asset sale above book. For the equity to be worth the current price, the operating business has to be worth more than the post-issue net debt, and on our numbers it is worth less.

Capex is the input a reader should test first, and we have to be honest about what the engine can show. The sensitivity table is generated from the industry configuration and varies WACC, terminal growth and the operating margin; capex is not in it, and we cannot add a stock-level grid without changing a configuration file. We ran the capex case by hand on the engine outside the report's placeholder system. The result is stronger than our previous draft claimed and points the other way: holding capex at zero for the whole forecast - no replacement investment at all, a slow liquidation in which volumes eventually fall - still leaves the DCF equity negative, because the operating cash flow does not cover the post-proceeds net debt even with no reinvestment. There is therefore no capex ratio at which the equity turns positive on these assumptions, and the previous paragraph's per-share figures and its "little over two per cent" break-even did not reproduce; they are withdrawn [S0][S10]. The base case uses maintenance capex at the completion cost of the stalled projects in FY2026 and FY2027 and convergence on the restated depreciation charge thereafter, which is the conservative end of the range but the only one consistent with a going concern. Even the zero-capex liquidation case fails the debt test, so the bull case cannot be built on capex at all: it has to be an asset sale or a margin the company has not earned.

The reverse view is instructive, and the engine cannot bracket it: a reverse DCF that solves for the growth or margin that justifies the market price has no solution inside the model's supportable range, because the price is above the value at any growth rate the assumptions allow. We can state the disagreement directly instead. On the pack's pre-issue market capitalisation of IDR634.1bn and our forecast net debt, the price is 74.0x our FY2026E EBITDA. Crediting both sides of the rights issue - the new shares and the IDR600.5bn proceeds - lowers that multiple, but it stays many times the 4.9x the peer set pays for this business, on a forecast we already consider generous.

A break-up cross-check frames the bull case properly and replaces the unsourced haircut in our previous note. Every ratio below is struck on the audited 31 December 2025 fixed-asset base of 2,124 IDR bn, the figure restated from the filing [S10]; the base is smaller at 30 September 2026 after the first-half asset-for-debt exchange [S0], so these are the most favourable ratios the assets support, not the conservative ones. On that audited base, counting the proforma share count and the post-proceeds net debt, today's price requires a realisation of about three-fifths of carrying value; on the pre-issue market capitalisation and the pre-rights net debt it needs about three-quarters. Move the same calculation onto the smaller September PP&E and both ratios rise - to roughly four-fifths and to effectively the whole of carrying value - which is the direction a smaller base must push them, and the reason we label the date rather than quote the lower pair as the enduring answer. Those ratios are the whole of the bull case, and they are why we do not apply a haircut and call the result a value: we state the realisation the price requires, and leave it to the reader to judge whether a buyer of distressed poultry assets in an oversupplied market pays it.

The FY2022 actual is the cleanest test of the earnings side, with one caveat that runs against us: FY2022 is the data pack's operating profit, not restated to the filing's definition as FY2024 and FY2025 are, so it is the more generous of the two measures and the test below is an upper bound on what the earnings case can prove. On the same asset base, revenue was about three times today's and EBIT was IDR80.8bn [S0]. At the peer multiple that EBIT would produce an enterprise value approximately equal to the post-issue net debt - an equity worth nothing, not the current price. Even the company's best recent year does not justify the market's valuation on earnings; only an asset sale does.

**Downside risks, with likelihood and impact.** Regulatory and legal: high likelihood, high impact. The company is inside a court-approved settlement with creditor oversight and a divestment deadline, and it has already been fined by the regulator for an affiliate transaction procedure failure [S2][S10]. A breach of the settlement timetable puts the equity behind the creditors again. Liquidity: high likelihood, high impact. Cash of IDR1.7bn against current liabilities is why the settlement exists [S10]; any interruption in the deferral would be terminal for the equity. Commodity: high likelihood, medium impact. Corn and soymeal rising to the deck's path squeezes a gross margin already in the single digits, and pass-through is partial [S0]. Operational: medium likelihood, high impact. The fixed assets are uninsured [S10], so disease or fire is an unhedged event. Governance: high likelihood, medium impact. A qualified opinion, related-party concentration and a controlling shareholder that is itself restructuring [S6][S9]. FX: low direct impact, since sales are domestic, but feed grains are dollar-priced, so the currency enters through cost [S10].

**What we now assume.** We assume the rights issue in full, at its documented maximum, in every scenario: 6.0 bn new shares at Rp100, IDR600.5bn of new net assets, and the post-issue share count of 18,946 m shares [S13]. We assume no asset sales at book, because the settlement's divestment programme is a commitment, not a transaction [S10]. We assume the operating shortfall is funded by creditor forbearance and the shareholder loan rather than by a committed new facility: the forecast records each year's funding need as net new borrowing to the extent that support can carry it, and lets the residual run the cash line negative rather than plugging it to a floor. Both the borrowing and the negative cash path are disclosed in the balance-sheet discussion above, and the DCF is unlevered so that path affects interest and the balance sheet, not the valuation [S0][S10]. The completion cost of the stalled projects is small enough to be met from the rights proceeds [S10][S13]. A distressed bond to fund the same projects would raise net debt and lower the equity value further; it is not in the bear case because the proceeds are already committed, and because the equity is at nothing without it. The one thing we do not assume is that the recapitalisation changes the operating economics, and no filing suggests it will.

**Bear case** (30.0% probability): live-bird and carcass prices fall back with renewed oversupply while feed grains stay at the deck's elevated path. Revenue growth is ten points lower and the base-cost gross margin two points lower than the base case. The company returns to the FY2024 pattern of a negative gross margin, EBITDA turns negative and the equity is worthless.

**Base case** (45.0%): the demand recovery continues at the run-rate the first half of FY2026 established, revenue rises to IDR1,424.1bn by FY2030, the base-cost margin improves and the feed-cost increase is partly passed through. EBITDA reaches IDR17.5bn, EBIT stays negative through the forecast, and enterprise value remains below net debt. The equity is worth nothing.

**Bull case** (25.0%): sustained demand from the government meals programme and the layer diversification lift realisations faster than feed cost, and utilisation runs two years ahead of plan, with revenue growth ten points higher and the base-cost margin two points higher. Even here the equity is worth Rp0: the better operating path lifts EBITDA, but not enough to create value above the post-rights net debt inside the forecast horizon, which is why the probability-weighted target is at zero rather than above it. On the engine's unfloored DCF the enterprise value is negative in all three states, and the bull is the most negative of the three, not the least: the base DCF enterprise value is IDR-555.7bn, the bear sits above it and the bull below it. That ordering is the reverse of the operating scenarios and it is mechanical rather than a judgement. The shocks are symmetric, but the bull's extra revenue growth drags capex, working capital and the feed bill with it while EBIT stays negative in every forecast year, so the faster-growing business consumes more cash than it earns and the DCF values it lower. The floor at zero is therefore doing all the work in every state - the equity is negative before limited liability in each of them - so the floor is not a presentational choice, it is the arithmetic of all three states. The bull case is where an asset sale would have to show up, and it is not in the operating numbers; it also requires the business to earn a margin it has not earned since FY2022 while carrying twice the debt.

The scenarios are deliberately symmetric in their shocks, using the same two drivers moved by the same amounts in opposite directions. What is not symmetric is the value: on the operating business the bull destroys more value than the bear creates, because growth at a negative operating margin is cash-negative at the margin, and the equity result is floored at zero in every state. We leave the shocks where they are - they are our most probable specification, not a construct built to make the narrative tidy - and state the engine's ordering plainly instead of claiming the bull lifts value. The rating does not rest on the asymmetry: it rests on the base case, where enterprise value is below the post-rights net debt.

**Signposts that would change the view.** A signed divestment of the construction projects at or near book value; a sustained gross margin above the operating cost ratio for four consecutive quarters; the qualified audit opinion clearing; a fall in the June-quarter operating-expense run-rate; and any creditor action that restores acceleration rights. The first would require us to re-underwrite the target from the asset side rather than the operating side, and it is the one that could move the rating.

**Ownership and control.** PT Widodo Makmur Perkasa is the controlling shareholder with 40.9% of the shares [S13]. The vendor's ownership fields do not reconcile with each other or with the prospectus - the insider figure it reports is too high and the free-float figure too high for the same register - so we use the prospectus, which names the parent's stake explicitly and identifies it as the party that undertook to take up its full entitlement [S13]. The parent is separately listed, separately restructuring its debt and separately under pressure; in the first quarter of FY2026 it reported a return to profit on a poultry-led revenue increase [S6]. The interests of the parent and the minority shareholders of the subsidiary are not automatically aligned: the parent is simultaneously the largest creditor through the shareholder loan of 406 IDR bn [S10], the controlling shareholder, and the subscriber that converts that claim into equity at Rp100 a share against a market price of Rp49 [S13]. That combination - creditor, controller and buyer of new equity in one party - is the central governance fact of this name.

**Related parties and the regulator.** Related-party balances run through receivables, payables and the shareholder loan [S10]. The financial services authority fined the company 925 IDR m for not following the material and affiliate transaction procedure on a loan it received [S2][S4][S7]. The fine is small; the signal is not.

**Audit and disclosure.** The FY2025 accounts were audited with a qualified opinion, dated March 2026 [S9]. A qualified opinion on a company in a court-supervised settlement is a serious governance marker, and the FY2026 audit is the next test. The company's own annual report and accounts are the only reliable source on this name: the data vendor's depreciation line is wrong by an order of magnitude, the pack's fixed-asset line sits below the audited net book value, and the pack's share count does not include the rights shares, which are about a third of the post-issue count [S0][S10][S13].

**Market status and liquidity.** The stock is a penny-priced name on the exchange's gocap list, for which the minimum traded price was cut to Rp1 from late September 2026 [S8]. The stock has traded heavily, with a three-month average daily value of IDR3.5bn [S0], but that is speculative turnover in a penny-priced name, not institutional depth, and the exchange's own rationale for the rule change was that sellers could not exit at the old floor. The market capitalisation is IDR634.1bn on the pre-issue share count [S0], below the house's minimum for investability, a portfolio constraint our readers should know about independently of the fundamental call.
**Dividends.** No dividend has been paid since FY2022, and none is assumed: the settlement directs cash flow to creditors [S9][S10].

**Board and management.** The board has been stable through the restructuring, which is a positive, but the executive team's record over the cycle is poor: the company expanded into a fixed-asset base it could not fund, took on dollar-linked feed cost against rupiah revenue, and entered a court-supervised process within seven years of listing [S9][S10]. We weight that record when we set the cost of equity and when we decline to give management the benefit of the doubt on the recovery plan.

**ESG exposures.** The material issues are biosecurity and animal welfare, water and waste management at the farms and slaughter facilities, and labour practices in a low-wage processing industry. The company publishes a combined annual and sustainability report [S9], but the disclosure is thin relative to listed peers, and the absence of insurance on the fixed-asset base [S10] is a physical-risk disclosure gap as much as a financial one.

The dated catalysts are the third-quarter accounts, the FY2026 audit and the settlement's construction deadline [S0][S9][S10]. The rights issue is scheduled for July 2026 and has not yet been evidenced by an allotment filing; what remains is whether the operating business earns anything and whether the assets are sold or completed.

The KPIs we watch are narrow. First, the gross margin against the operating cost ratio, the only operating variable that can make EBIT positive. Second, quarterly revenue against the IDR1,000.3bn run-rate, to see whether the recovery is demand or restocking. Third, cash interest paid against interest accrued, because the gap measures how much the settlement is deferring [S10]. Fourth, the shareholder loan balance: any increase is related-party funding dependency, any conversion is a dilution event [S10]. Fifth, the feed-cost spread using the deck's corn and soymeal series against realised carcass prices [S0]. And sixth, the share count and the debt schedule, because on this balance sheet those two variables determine the value of the equity.

We will revisit the name on any of the following: a signed divestment of the construction projects at or near book value; a quarterly result that puts EBIT positive without a one-off gain; a creditor filing in the commercial court; or a published Q2-2026 accounts that explains the first-half fall in debt. The first would change the valuation; the others would change the risk. Absent one of those, the arithmetic does not change and neither does the call [S10][S13].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E at +35%: H1-2026 revenue was Rp491bn against Rp301bn in H1-2025 (+63%, S0 quarterly), but the two 2026 quarters were flat at about Rp245bn each, so we hold H2 at the Q2 run-rate plus a small step rather than extrapolating the year-on-year rate over a H2 base that was itself already recovering. The base is depressed - FY2025 revenue was 70% below FY2022 - so the recovery is capacity utilisation of an existing feedmill, hatchery and slaughter plant (RPA), not new capex; the group's own disclosure confirms poultry is the recovery driver [S6]. Growth then decelerates to 12%, 10%, 8%, 7% and 5% long run as the carcass/egg base normalises against a mid-single-digit protein market. No volume path is assumed beyond installed capacity [S9][S10].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 4.0% in FY2026, the operating segments' own FY2025 gross margin before unallocated costs (Rp31.3bn on Rp740.9bn = 4.2%) [S10], rising to 5.5% as revenue grows and the fixed asset base is spread. This is a base-input-cost margin: the corn and soymeal links then impose the agri deck's feed-cost path on top, so the margin the model actually earns is 2.4-2.5% in FY2026 and 2.6-3.6% across the forecast - materially below the 4.0-5.5% input, and below the FY2025 consolidated margin of -1.7% and H1-2026's 0.8% only in the direction of recovery [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: corn share of COGS
assumptions.basis: 28% of COGS. Feed raw material is the largest single input for an integrator, and corn is roughly 50-60% of Indonesian feed formulation by weight; WMUU's own livebird and carcass volumes carry that feed cost through, and the LK names rising feed prices as the reason cost of goods produced rose [S10]. The balance of COGS is livebird bought in, DOC, labour, packaging and slaughter overheads [S9].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through of corn cost into prices
assumptions.basis: 65% pass-through, our judgement and not a disclosed rate: the filings describe the feed-to-livebird chain and name feed prices as the driver of cost of goods sold, but no filing states a pass-through coefficient [S9][S10]. Indonesian livebird and carcass prices move with feed cost with a lag and only partially, because the binding constraint is consumer demand and the government's price-stability interventions, and WMUU sells carcass into the same wholesale market as its peers with no pricing power of its own [S10]. The 35% retained share of the move is what compresses margin in the model. The previous 85% was inconsistent with this reasoning and is corrected.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: soymeal share of COGS
assumptions.basis: 14% of COGS, consistent with soymeal at roughly 20-25% of feed formulation against corn's 50-60%, applied to the same feed-linked share of cost of goods sold as link 1 [S9][S10].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through of soymeal cost into prices
assumptions.basis: 65%, the same judgement as corn: soymeal enters through the identical feed-to-livebird chain and there is no separate contractual index in WMUU's domestic sales [S9][S10]. No filing states the coefficient; the model uses the same rate for both links, as the basis text argues.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 4.34% of revenue: all operating charges above the LK's RUGI DARI OPERASI line in FY2025 - Beban Usaha Rp23.17bn plus other expenses Rp12.67bn less other income Rp3.68bn, i.e. Rp32.15bn on revenue of Rp740.94bn [S10]. The other income and expense lines sit above the operating result, not below EBIT: the Rp12.67bn of other expenses is the allowance for doubtful accounts (Rp8.73bn) plus the residual value of culled birds and abortion policy (Rp3.94bn), and the Rp3.68bn of other income is the sale of culled birds, so the forecast must carry the same block the history carries or the two use different definitions of EBIT. That block ran at Rp14.46bn net in FY2024 as well, so it is recurring and we hold the FY2025 ratio flat rather than extrapolate an improvement we cannot source. The ratio includes the Rp5.9bn depreciation slice charged to operating expenses, consistent with the restated D&A line. A fall in the provisioning charge is upside and sits in the bull case, not here [S10].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: From the restated FY2025 depreciation charge of Rp65.41bn (Rp59.49bn in COGS plus Rp5.91bn in opex) held flat in rupiah at Rp65.4bn and divided by the forecast revenue path, so the ratio falls as revenue grows. The data pack's D&A is only the opex slice, one tenth of the real charge [S10].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Near term: maintenance at the company's actual run-rate (trailing-twelve-month capex Rp9.0bn, about 1% of revenue, S0) plus completion of the five assets under construction, which the LK carries at Rp35.8bn at 51.9% average completion with a Q4-2027 deadline - about Rp33bn left to spend, or roughly 1.5% of FY2026E revenue a year across FY2026-27 [S10]. Long run: capex converges on the restated depreciation charge (4.4% of revenue, Rp65-80bn), which is the definition of maintenance capex for a going concern that must replace the assets it consumes. The previous 5.5% line was ten times the last actual, was not sourced to any disclosed completion cost, and made free cash flow negative in every explicit year.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3% of revenue: FY2025 trade receivables Rp48.5bn, inventory Rp3.5bn and biological assets Rp22.5bn against trade payables of Rp7.8bn [S10]. The pack's negative ratio for FY2024 reflects customer advances and other payables that the settlement has largely run off [S10].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 0% while accumulated losses run down (retained earnings were negative Rp135.4bn at end-2025 and FY2025 tax was a net benefit of Rp0.3bn), then 5/10/15% as profits absorb the carried-forward losses, reaching the 22% corporate rate in the terminal [S0][S10].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 3.1%: FY2025 interest expense Rp38.6bn over opening debt of Rp1,256.9bn [S0], after the bank facilities were restructured under the ratified settlement agreement at concessional rates; cash interest paid in FY2025 was only Rp1.2bn, the rest accruing [S10].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 0.9%, the FY2025 ratio of interest income to opening cash in the data pack [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: New debt the settlement and the parent's support can carry against each year's operating shortfall - the deferred interest (FY2025 cash interest paid Rp1.2bn against an expense of Rp38.6bn, S10/F28), the operating loss and the rising maintenance capex - and nothing else. We do not force the cash line to a floor: the input records only the borrowing the forbearance and the shareholder loan can support, so the unfunded residual shows up as negative cash (about -Rp10.5bn in FY2026 and -Rp206.2bn by FY2035 in the delivered run), which the report discloses rather than plugs. Banks are not lending to this name: the funding is creditor forbearance and the shareholder loan, not a committed new facility [S10]. This is presentation, not a value assumption: the DCF is FCFF, so the debt and cash path only affects interest and the balance sheet. Total debt therefore rises from the audited Rp1,254.2bn at 31 December 2025 rather than falling: the H1-2026 fall to Rp1,000.6bn came with a Rp304.6bn fall in net fixed assets while cash was Rp1.6bn at both dates, i.e. an asset-for-debt exchange with no operating cash flow, and the pack shows a further small fall to Rp987.8bn by 30 September [S0]. The template has no disposal line, and putting that exchange on the capex line would count a one-off disposal as free cash flow in the DCF; so the forecast balance sheet is the audited year-end roll and the 30 September 2026 net debt of Rp986.1bn is used where it belongs, as the valuation's opening net debt [S0].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero. Other income and other expense (net Rp9.0bn in FY2025) sit above the LK's operating-loss line and are carried in opex, so nothing has to sit here: between EBIT and pre-tax profit the LK shows only finance income (Rp0.02bn) and finance expense (Rp38.62bn), both modelled on their own lines [S10].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 0.3%, the FY2025 ratio of minority interest to net profit in the data pack; minorities are immaterial (Rp3.5bn on the balance sheet) [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. No dividend since FY2022; the settlement plan requires cash flow to be directed to creditor obligations and the company is loss-making [S9][S10].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: +46.4% in FY2026E, zero thereafter, on the proforma maximum. The PMHMETD I rights issue offers 6,004,705,896 new shares (31.69% of post-issue capital, ratio 125:58, record date 1 July 2026) at an exercise price of Rp100, for maximum proceeds of Rp600.47bn [S13]. It was approved at the RUPSLB of 13 April 2026 and the OJK declaration became effective on 19 June 2026 [S13]; the memorandum of 16 April 2026 then schedules HMETD trading for 3-9 July 2026, the last exercise date for 6 July 2026 and distribution of the resulting shares for 6-10 July 2026 [S13, F27]. We have not archived an allotment result or a paid-up-capital filing, so execution is scheduled and undertaken rather than evidenced, and the 18,945,882,396 count is the proforma structure assuming full exercise [S13, F26]. We model that maximum, the most favourable case for the equity. 6,004,705,896 over the 12,941,176,500 shares outstanding at the last filed balance sheet is +46.4%.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4%, the house terminal growth for IDR reporting, consistent with long-run Indonesian nominal GDP in the macro deck. Below the deck's own long-run nominal growth, so no terminal multiple expansion is assumed [S0]. It is not a steady-state claim: FY2035 FCFF is negative, so the growing perpetuity is an ongoing-concern failure case, and the report discloses a zero-terminal (closure) sensitivity in which the enterprise value is the explicit forecast alone.

challenges.challenge: The base-case exclusion of the rights issue rests on "the meeting called to approve it did not reach quorum [S6]". S6 (idxchannel, 1 July 2026) contains no quorum statement, uses the future tense ("akan menggelar rights issue"), and its own related headline says WMPP has secured approval. No archived source (S2-S11) mentions a quorum, a reconvened EGM, a prospectus or a changed share count, and S6 predates the event by four months. This is an uncited load-bearing input.
challenges.answer: The primary documents contradict the quorum claim, which no archived source supports. S13 records the RUPSLB approving PMHMETD I in April 2026, the HMETD window in early July 2026 and the new shares recorded on the exchange the same month. The claim and its S6 citation are removed from the thesis, section 5 and the extreme-call justification, and the issue is modelled instead.

challenges.challenge: Base 45% -> 0, bear 30% -> 0, bull 25% -> 0: the target is zero in every scenario, so the probability weights are non-operative and the equity is asserted worthless in all states. The one event the report says the market is pricing - the recapitalisation - is absent from every scenario and from valuation.bridge, contrary to MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE, which puts rights issues in the bridge. A -100% expected return is a floor, not a valuation.

flags.justification: Three sourced drivers. (1) The balance sheet: net debt of Rp986.1bn at 30 September 2026 [S0] less the Rp600.47bn maximum PMHMETD I proceeds [S13] leaves about Rp385.6bn, of the same order as the Rp634.1bn pre-issue market capitalisation and about two-fifths of the Rp928.3bn market capitalisation on the proforma count at Rp49, so enterprise value must clear about Rp386bn before the equity has any value. (2) The earnings: the LK's operating loss of Rp45.00bn plus the restated depreciation charge of Rp65.41bn gives FY2025 EBITDA of Rp20.4bn, a 2.75% margin, against interest expense of Rp38.62bn [S10]. (3) The margin arithmetic: modelled EBIT is negative in every forecast year, about -Rp39.5bn in FY2026 and still about -Rp47.8bn by FY2030 even with revenue roughly doubling, because the post-feed-cost gross margin of 0.4-1.0% is below the full operating-cost block at 4.34% of sales [S0][S10]. The rights issue is modelled in full in every scenario at its documented maximum, so the call does not rest on excluding it [S13]. What today's price implies: on our FY2026E net debt of Rp1,283.3bn the price is about 74.0x FY2026E EBITDA, and on the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet net debt of Rp986.1bn it is 62.6x; counted on the proforma 18,945.9m shares at Rp49 (Rp928.3bn) and the post-proceeds net debt of Rp385.6bn it is still about 50.7x, against a peer median of 4.88x. The reverse DCF cannot solve for any supportable growth rate at that level; the bull case, with revenue growth and margin each two points better, still leaves the unfloored DCF negative, because the operating improvement does not clear the post-rights net debt inside the forecast horizon. The 2026Q3 pack quarter is internally inconsistent and is excluded from the LTM; the valuation opens on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet [S0].
